newsitem.title: USA: Stockpile cobalt sales likely from August - trade.
newsitem.headline: Stockpile cobalt sales likely from August - trade.

text.p: Cobalt sales from the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center were likely to restart in August following this week's court ruling which lifted a restraining order, thus paving the way for the government to re-enter the market, strategic metals dealers said.
"I would like to think it's July and August (for sales), but I don't think they can get their act together that fast," said one cobalt merchant in New York.
Dealers estimated that Stockpile will likely offer 500,000 pounds in August and another one million pounds in September.
Stockpile administrator Richard Connelly said on June 24 that the agency will make an announcement shortly regarding its sales timetable.

The Stockpile sales are free to resume after the U.S. Court of Federal Claims on June 18 lifted an injunction that had been granted at the request of Minor Metals Inc, a trading company which filed complaints in two separate U.S. courts over how Stockpile sold its hoard of the strategic metal.

Stockpile said this week that the "all or none" clause in cobalt sales will remain, despite Minor Metals' complaints, but the domestic preference clause, also subject of complaint, will be removed from the next sealed bid sale.
Dealers said the inclusion of the domestic preference clause had allowed some U.S. consumers to submit low bids, and later match higher bids presented by those who wanted to export the metal.
"The domestic preference did not affect (Stockpile's) revenue because domestic bidders were forced to match the export price anyway," the New York cobalt merchant said.
"It just gave some people who wanted to keep it here domestically an advantage. But was this domestic versus exportable worth a 12-week shutdown? Probably not," he said.
A spokesmen for Minor Metals in the U.S. could not be reached for comment. A spokesman for its allied company in London, Metal Resources Group, declined comment on its court filings.

Stockpile has authority to sell 6 million lbs of cobalt in the current fiscal year, and has already sold about 2.1 million lbs. A further 6 million lbs will be up for grabs in the next fiscal year beginning October 1.

Most of the low grade cobalt in the Stockpile's warehouses has been exhausted, and the next round of sales were likely to be metal grading 99.3 to 99.65 percent cobalt, competing with Russian and Zambian output, dealers said.
Prices of the lower-grade Russian cobalt have actually risen a touch this week, while Western grade metal was unchanged, dealers said.
Stockpile also has higher grades which compete with the best Western metal produced by Inco, Falconbridge and others.
Stockpile sold its lower grade metal first when the market was tight, keeping the best for later to compete more effectively when cobalt supplies were expected to increase.
"It's a rare event that the government did something that was correct," a second cobalt merchant commented.
Western grade cobalt was quoted by dealers mid-range at $22.00 a lb, with Russian grade at $19.00 to $19.25 a lb.
Dealers felt that striking workers at Inco Ltd in Sudbury, Ontario, were likely to settle when they vote again on a revised package Saturday.
On August 1, Falconbridge's labor contract covering 1,700 workers at Sudbury expires. Nevertheless, some merchants believed they were likely to settle in line with terms agreed at Inco.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1646))
